newsitem.title: USA: Q4 steel earnings expected down on weak pricing.
newsitem.headline: Q4 steel earnings expected down on weak pricing.

text.p: Most U.S. integrated steelmakers are expected to post lower earnings for the 1996 fourth quarter and full year due to soft contract prices, which could signal long-term profitability problems in an industry with perhaps too many players, analysts said.
"Everyone will be down because of (lower) contract pricing with the exception of USX-U.S. Steel Group," said Chuck Bradford at UBS Securities.
U.S. Steel posted nonrecurring charges in the fourth quarter of 1995, dampening earnings.
"The industry is well below the level of profitability it needs to survive. I think it means the industry is in for some long-term problems," Bradford warned.

Bradford said there are too many steelmakers seeking annual supply contracts with a small number of customers, primarily the three major U.S. automakers, General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp.

That has given automakers more leverage in contract negotiations and the ability to keep a cap on prices they pay for steel. "There should be three big steel companies serving the contract customers," Bradford said.
Supply contracts with auto and appliance makers can account for half of a steel company's business in many cases.
Analysts said contract prices were down 3 to 4 percent in '96 versus '95, although steel demand last year was surprisingly strong.

"I think the demand in '96 surprised a lot of people," said Tom Abrams at First Boston. Industry shipments are expected to come in close to 100 million tons in '96, compared with 95 million tons in '95.
Abrams said he expects contract prices to be flat this year.
"There are a lot of people chasing the business...it's just very competitive," Abrams said.
Industry officials, while declining to comment on prices, said demand should stay strong this year and industry shipments could again reach 100 million tons.
"Like Yogi Berra once said, it's deja vu all over again," said Paul Wilhelm, president of U.S. Steel. "We expect the market to be about the same as '96."
Wilhelm said automakers have projected they will build 15 million vehicles this year, about the same as last year.
